## Title Page

# FAT-CAT for Explainability and Augmentation for an AI System: A Case Study on the AI Recruitment System Adoption

5 ChangHyun Lee<sup>a</sup>, KyungJin Cha<sup>a\*</sup>

<sup>a</sup>Hanyang University, 222, Wangsimni-ro, Seongdong-gu, Seoul, Republic of Korea

## Abstract

Because artificial intelligence (AI) recruitment systems exhibited discriminatory decisions in recent applications, the adoption of such systems in industry has raised doubts. As equity has been emphasized in AI decision-making frameworks, the non-explainability issue regarding the high performance of AI methods has become prominent. Therefore, scholars have focused on human–AI augmentation in which humans consider equity and AI supports the consideration. As a result, explainability is highlighted as a new capability of AI methods for an ideal decision. In this regard, this study proposes the so-called fairness, accountability, and transparency (FAT)-complexity, anxiety, and trust (CAT) model that describes the path from explainability to AI system adoption considering augmentation, assuming that the capability of the AI decision maker to explain the basis of its decision and interact with the human decision maker is crucial for AI recruitment system adoption. We found that explainability and augmentation are two key factors in AI recruitment system adoption and assessed that their importance will gradually increase as recruiters will be asked to use such AI systems more commonly. Moreover, this study conceptualized the role of an augmented relationship

1 between humans and AI in decision-making, in which they complement each other’s

2 limitations.

3 **Keywords:** Explainability, human–AI augmentation, technology adoption, AI system,

4 digital transformation.

## 1. Introduction

Decision makers have been prompted to consider both efficiency and equity in their

decisions: efficiency focuses on quantitative cost effectiveness, while equity focuses on

qualitative equality for equal needs (Correia, 1999; James et al., 2005). However, artificial

5 intelligence (AI) systems have been commonly constructed considering efficiency rather than

6 equity owing to their black-box construction, which makes it difficult to track their causal

relationship (London, 2019). Although deep learning algorithms are not capable of providing

the underpinnings of their decisions, they have been commonly adopted because they attain

high prediction performance (Adadi & Berrada, 2018). However, in cases where critical

problems occurred because of the AI system, which does not consider equity, the importance

of AI decision makers considering equity was highlighted. For example, Amazon is known to

have scrapped its AI recruitment tool because it was biased toward male applicants (Reuters,

2018). At present, the algorithm is required to have not only a high accuracy but also make an

unbiased decision. In this regard, firms have tried to justify whether their AI-based decisions

satisfy certain qualitative virtues (London, 2019), and studies on AI have shifted their focus

from learning performance (i.e., prediction accuracy or learning time) to equity, such as

equality and minimizing human bias (Arrieta et al., 2020).

Furthermore, there have been several attempts to address the bias issue of AI

recruitment systems but none have completely solved it. For instance, Microsoft has

developed Fairlearn and InterpretML, and Eric Rosenblum has developed the Second Look to

assess the fairness of their model and mitigate bias (Thomson Reuters, 2021). Because AI

systems are rooted in statistical and linear algebra computations, considering justifications,

which are difficult to measure quantitatively, is more difficult than considering performance.

Therefore, recent studies have considered justification, explaining whether the expert system actions are reasonable for the common good, as the role of a human decision maker. Instead, explainability, which is defined as the ability of the AI to provide information about what the algorithm is doing, has been suggested as an additional role of an AI decision maker to support human decisions (London, 2019). Accordingly, human–AI augmentation in which an explainable AI (XAI) framework explains the AI decision-making processes and humans justify the final decision, has become a key condition for an ideal decision-making process (Duan et al., 2019; Teodorescu et al., 2021). In other words, regardless of its performance, AI is difficult to be adopted if it lacks explainability, which allows augmentation. Subsequently, this study raised the following research questions: (1) Is AI explainability a prerequisite for human–AI augmentation? (2) Can augmentation features be applied as an AI system adoption criterion? (3) Can augmentation features be representative of AI recruitment system adoption features?

To review these research questions, this study proposes the so-called fairness, accountability, and transparency (FAT)-complexity, anxiety, and trust (CAT) model to assess AI systems in terms of explainability and augmentation. The FAT-CAT model is constructed with three attributes regarding explainability (namely, fairness, accountability, and transparency (FAT)) and three attributes regarding augmentation (namely, complexity, anxiety, and trust (CAT)). We review the existing literature to demonstrate the validity of the FAT-CAT model in Section 2 and propose the hypotheses for examining the research questions in Section 3. Then, we propose the method in Section 4 and analyze the data based on the proposed method in Section 5. Finally, we present the findings and limitations of the proposed method in Section 6 and draw brief conclusions in Section 7.

## 2. Literature Review

## 24 2.1. AI Recruitment Systems

As information technology has advanced to the point where AI is commonly applied in workplaces, the decision-making processes in various fields and industries, such as human resource recruitment (Ochmann & Laumer, 2019; Laurim et al., 2021) and healthcare (Ahsen et al., 2019; Panch et al., 2019), have been increasingly relying on AI systems. Although AI applications were initially expected to automate human labor, provide information to humans, and transform business processes (Dehning et al., 2003), recent AI systems are capable of autonomously taking over an entire work process instead of simply automating human labor and making autonomous decisions without human interaction instead of providing information to the human decision maker (Stritch et al., 2021). Studies attracted by the outstanding performance of sophisticated AI systems have tended to focus more on efficiency, even if these systems cannot explain causality (London, 2019; Stritch et al., 2021). However, recent studies point out several problems that may occur when a perspective solely focused on the performance is applied to practical cases. For example, Arrieta et al. (2020) conceptualized these problems as two gaps: The application gap is defined as a digital transformation delay for reasons such as difficulty in predicting the adverse effects that may occur when an AI system is applied to the industry, even though the AI system is technologically prepared. The knowledge gap occurs when a decision maker has more information and knowledge, even though the interests of the decision maker and stakeholders are different.

AI recruitment is a representative field that needs to consider these problems when applying AI decision makers. AI systems support various recruitment processes by automatically evaluating applicants, providing information to the recruiters and applicants, and transforming how people search and advertise for jobs (Laurim et al., 2021). Although the advanced technology of AI recruitment systems has been actively developed, an ethical issue has also been addressed recently (Ochmann & Laumer, 2019). For example, the

Amazon case has highlighted the application gap as Amazon postponed the adoption of its 2 system owing to the potential adverse effects of biased AI recruitment systems and concerns 3 regarding fairness. Moreover, the AI recruitment field has shown a knowledge gap, as 4 applicants may desire to know the reason behind recruitment decisions but recruiters have 5 less capability to track the rationale of the AI decision maker’s operation and are not 6 obligated to disclose it (Kim & Heo, 2021).

To mitigate these gaps, scholars have suggested that each stakeholder (i.e., researchers, recruiters, and applicants) should understand that each other’s interests are different and actively mediate them (Kim & Heo, 2021; Laurim et al., 2021). For example, recruiters were interested in the malfunction of the algorithm that can decrease the number of competitive applicants, which is difficult to handle. Recruitment experts were interested in whether an AI recruitment system could function ethically, without discrimination and considering diversity, and whether it could explain its process to allow modifications (Ochmann & Laumer, 2019). AI recruitment systems are also expected to yield high and reliable performance owing to the anxiety of losing valuable talents and be constructed using easy, controllable, and trialable algorithms to handle these adverse effects (Laurim et al., 2021). On the other hand, applicants are mainly affected by internal motivational features. For instance, they are influenced by usefulness, novelty of activity, attitude, anxiety, trust, enjoyment, and being able to confirm their own results immediately after using an AI recruitment system (Eveleth et al., 2015; Van Esch et al., 2019; Laurim et al., 2021). The role of human decision makers is being emphasized in mediating these different motivations. Furthermore, the explainability of AI to support human decision-making is emerging.

## 2.2. Human–AI Augmentation

The awe and fear of the capability of AI systems is an obsolete but everlasting topic.

Some expect that efficient automation via AI applications will increase overall productivity, 2 while others worry that AI systems will replace human roles entirely owing to their high 3 efficiency (Chui et al., 2016; Stritch et al., 2021). These concerns are continuous because the 4 portfolio of AI applications has expanded to decision-making. However, recent studies have 5 differentiated the roles of human and AI decision makers (Duan et al., 2019). For example, 6 Green & Chen (2019) suggested an interactive loop framework in which AI decisions rely on 7 human labor, such as labeling and correcting errors, and human decision can be improved by 8 AI labor, such as identifying patterns and cleansing complex datasets. In other words, AI 9 decision makers can be used complements rather than substitutes for human decision makers 10 (Duan et al., 2019). These two actors are compatible such that the AI systems prepare the 11 basis for the decision and humans make the final decision (Sendak et al., 2020). Regarding 12 such human–AI augmentation, previous studies conceptualized three conditions in 13 which they cooperate with each other: complexity, uncertainty, and equivocality (Pich et al., 14 2002; Jarrahi, 2018).

Complexity is considered in both the management and computer science fields. The former views it as a dynamic situation caused by various and continuously changing external conditions (Snowden & Boone, 2007), while the latter views it as a computational complexity in terms of function size growth owing to the large number of features (Bossaerts & Murawski, 2017). information management systems field, dynamic situations are considered to have multi-dimensional features, which causes an increase in computational cost. That is, each complexity forms a vicious cycle that causes another complexity; however, scholars have explained that human–AI augmentation can minimize the occurrence of such phenomena (Jarrahi, 2018). Human decision makers can contribute to reducing computational complexity by selecting the appropriate data to feed the algorithm through their domain knowledge (e.g., feature selection), while AI decision makers can contribute to reducing the com lexit of humans b curatin and anal zin the ro osed data (e feature extraction) p y y g y g p p .g., .

Human–AI augmentation can improve decisions by recognizing valid conditions. Uncertainty refers to a lack of information when making decisions (Daft & Lengel, 1986). In the computer science field, uncertainty and complexity are often correlated as a trade-off depending on the amount of information (e.g., Gubian et al., 2008). However, they can also be considered in a compositive relationship in the information management system field. For example, if decision makers lack domain knowledge, they would struggle to recognize which complex conditions to focus on, consequently, may fail to find a direct cause of their research goal (Bostrom et al., 2015). To overcome the uncertain situation, AI decision makers can provide more real-time insight and information that can support rational decisions (e.g., data mining or anomaly detection), while human decision makers can make intuitive and heuristic decisions based on limited information (Jarrahi, 2018). AI decision makers can support human decision makers by providing more information, so that human decision makers make concrete decisions based on such additional information. Equivocality refers to ambiguity and possibility of multiple and conflicting interpretations in organizational decision-making (Daft & Lengel, 1986). Equivocality can occur when there is no clear consensus on the organization’s common goal (Pich et al., 2002), when there are conflicting interests between the stakeholders (Jarrahi, 2018) and issues are subjective (Frishammar et al., 2010). For example, human resource recruitment is equivocal because even if one recruiter determines an applicant appropriate for the organization, the other may assess the applicant differently. Equivocality makes problems multidirectional, increasing the variance of the decision, uncertain, complex, confusing, and chaotic (Frishammar et al., 2010; Blomme & Bornebroek-Te Lintelo, 2012). To mitigate equivocality, human decision makers should communicate with each other until they derive a consensus about the organizational direction (Blomme & Bornebroek-Te Lintelo, 2012), while the role of AI decision makers is to provide information from various angles so that human decision makers can engage in discussions considering various perspectives (Jarrahi, 2018).

## 2.3. Explainability

Explainability in AI is defined as the ability to explain how an algorithm works and why it has delivered particular outcomes (Shin, 2021). In contrast to accuracy, which does not depend on the decision maker, explainability originates from the perspective that the roles of humans and AI systems in decision-making are different. Previous studies suggested FAT as characteristics of explainability, which highlight the role of humans in decision-making (Adadi & Berrada, 2018). Fairness refers to procedural fairness, which considers diverse social status and faiths (Chiu et al., 2009; Ochmann & Laumer, 2019). This approach argues that decisions made by the algorithm should not be influenced by various discriminatory factors, such as race, gender, and religion (Ochmann & Laumer, 2019). However, because the algorithm trains with human-generated data, it inherits human bias and prejudice (Ahsen et al., 2019). Subsequently, unfair decisions frequently occur because they are often affected by the human decision maker’s subjectivity. For example, because human-generated recruitment decisions were influenced by age and gender, AI generated decisions may also yield biased decisions based on the applicant’s age and gender (Ochmann & Laumer, 2019). Unlike AI decision makers, human decision makers are responsible not to overlook vulnerable populations (Sendak et al., 2020). Accordingly, explainability can contribute to fairness by offering opportunities to recruiters to recognize and adjust the biases and prejudices to not be considered (Abdul et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019). Accountability denotes the responsibility of humans to ensure that their work interests the common good, such as safety and privacy concerns (Diakopoulos, 2016). Accountability includes the following two concepts: controllability and openness. Controllability refers to the responsibility of the human decision maker to audit and modify the irrational configuration of the AI decision maker (Shin, 2021). In other words, accountability requires the human decision maker to control the negative impacts of the algorithm, such as discrimination and information leakage (Arrieta et al., 2020). As both fairness and controllability advocate non-discrimination, they can be interdependent regarding some aspects, but they differ in that the former mainly focuses on the purpose of not discriminating someone, while the latter mainly focuses on the capability of adjusting the outcome. On the other hand, openness allows non-experts to easily access the decision basis and understand how and why certain decisions were made (London, 2019). Most people who are influenced by the decision may desire to know the causal justifications behind a given result (Ochmann & Laumer, 2019). Openness requires providing a continuous and easy explanation to everyone about the decision process (Abdul et al., 2018). It mitigates the knowledge gap between the decision maker and stakeholder and can contribute to interactional fairness by showcasing the decision basis to the stakeholders (Chiu et al., 2009; Arrieta et al., 2020). Transparency helps human decision makers understand the algorithm by allowing them to simulate, decompose, and observe the model (Arrieta et al., 2020). Unlike AI decision makers, human decision makers desire to derive not only prediction values using the algorithm but also the insights that support their decision-making. Such explainability contributes to transparency by allowing to gain information and infer the causality between variables (Arrieta et al., 2020). For example, transparency not only indicates who is the most competitive applicant but also explains which capability makes the applicant the most competitive, which may provide more supportive insights to recruiters. Furthermore, transparency can act as a basis for fairness and accountability (Abdul et al., 2018). For instance, if transparency reveals that the capability that gave the applicant the competitive edge is a discriminatory feature, recruiters can subsequently adjust or control it. In this regard, transparency can lead to more confident and trustworthy decisions (Arrieta et al.,

2020).

## 3. Hypotheses Development

Explainability emphasizes the responsibility of human decision makers: fairness denotes the responsibility not to discriminate anyone, accountability denotes the responsibility to control the adverse effect of AI and disclose the decision basis to the stakeholders, and transparency denotes the responsibility to gain more information than classification or regression results (Arrieta et al., 2020; Sendak et al., 2020; Shin, 2021). In this regard, this study assumed that explainability has a positive effect on AI system adoption with the mediation of augmentation features and explainability can enhance the qualitative value of AI decision support. Therefore, this study urges recruiters to discover whether their AI system adoption is affected by explainability through the mediation of augmentation. However, we were cautious to construct a direct path from augmentation features to the AI recruitment system adoption because previous studies have only indirectly dealt with the concepts of augmentation features when adopting AI recruitment systems. Moreover, we were concerned that recruiters might not be familiar with the concepts of augmentation features because the AI recruitment systems are only recently being introduced. Therefore, to measure whether augmentation features can be representative of AI recruitment system adoption, this study replaced the attributes of human–AI augmentation with extended indicators; then, investigated the relationships between the AI recruitment adoption features and replaced indicators. In this section, we describe the reasoning behind replacing the augmentation features with the extended concepts and construct a conceptual model by considering the related AI recruitment adoption features utilized in previous studies. Table 1 describes the overall summary of the replacement from human-AI augmentation attributes to extended motivational indicators, and Figs 1 and 2 describe our proposed conceptual model.

## 3.1. Complexity

## 3.1.1. Replacing Complexity in Decision-Making with Technology Complexity

Complexity in decision-making is conceptualized as having too much information to consider (Jarrahi, 2018), while complexity in technology diffusion is defined as the perceived difficulty of using and understanding certain technologies (Rogers, 2010). If the recruiters perceive learning, using, or understanding the AI recruitment system difficult, the human decision-making process also becomes complex because AI recruitment adoption requires extra information and efforts (Pan et al., 2021). That is, although the role of the AI recruitment system is to reduce the amount of information to be considered, it can ironically increase complexity if the recruiters need to learn how to operate the AI system. For example, although an AI recruitment system can reduce unnecessary information by screening out ineligible applicants (Peña et al., 2020), aligning personal and work-based habits (Van Esch & Black, 2019) and confirming the validity of AI decision-making (Mujtaba & Mahapatra, 2019) requires significant information and effort. Therefore, recruiters may decide whether they will adopt the AI recruitment system depending on how the system affects complexity.

## H1a. Complexity will negatively affect AI recruitment adoption.

## 3.1.2. Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAT) for Complexity

When dealing with an AI recruitment system, recruiters experienced difficulty in interpreting and utilizing the results of the system rather than technical aspects (Laurim et al., 2021). Previous studies have suggested that the attributes of explainability can mitigate such difficulties. In terms of fairness, XAI can simplify the process of confirming whether the model functions fairly or ethically by visualizing the feature relations affecting a given result (Mujataba & Mahapatra, 2019). In terms of accountability, XAI can make it less complex to audit or redress biased AI decisions by revealing the decision basis (Arrieta et al., 2020). Finally, in terms of transparency, XAI can decrease the application gap by allowing scholars and AI representatives to directly explain the expected adverse effect of an AI recruitment system on recruiters. Based on these considerations, this study suggests that explainability can contribute to augmentation in terms of complexity.

**H1b. Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAT) will negatively affect complexity.**

## 3.2. Equivocality

## 3.2.1. Replacing Equivocality with Anxiety

Assessing applicants is often subjective because of the different interests, stakes, and perspectives of different recruiters (Pich et al., 2002; Frishammar et al., 2010; Jarrahi, 2018). Even applicant is classified as eligible for the organization by one recruiter, another recruiter may disagree with this assessment (Mujtaba & Mahapatra, 2019). In other words, recruitment results may involve the subjectivity of the scorer, and an AI recruitment system that trained on these results may be biased owing to the succession of subjectivity (Ahsen et al., 2019). Hence, applying an AI decision maker in a recruitment process may enhance the bias, even if the recruiters may request more objective decisions form the AI system.

In previous studies, this concern was reflected in the form of anxiety, which is defined as “the fear, apprehension, and hope people feel when considering using or using a new technology” (Meuter et al., 2003, pp. 900). As equivocality results in a multidirectional organizational goal, it hinders the AI recruitment system from seeking relevant features to concentrate (Mujtaba & Mahapatra, 2019). Consequently, recruiters fear losing valuable talent because of biased performance of the system (Laurim et al., 2021). In other words, recruiters may expect an AI recruitment system to decrease their anxiety by assisting their decision-making objectively; however, AI without explainability may not be objective because it inherits the human bias involved in its training data. Although the only way to prevent such anxiety is to discuss it thoroughly until a common agreement is reached, prior studies have pointed out that social anxiety may still arise during the communication process (Blomme & Bornebroek-Te Lintelo, 2012; Van Esch et al., 2019). Hence, this study assumed that anxiety will inevitably occur when adopting an AI recruitment system because of the equivocality issue.

## H2a. Anxiety will negatively affect AI recruitment adoption.

## 3.2.2. FAT in Relation to Anxiety

In a recruitment context, the subjectivity of the scorer may involve inapposite prejudice. XAI can contribute to reducing anxiety through incorporating fairness by informing the stakeholders of the prejudice involved (Ochmann & Laumer, 2019). Identification of prejudice helps recruiters to discuss more rationally and recruit candidates in a non-discriminatory manner (Frishammar et al., 2010). Recruiters who experience the fairness of the algorithm may be less anxious about losing competitive applicants (Daft & Lengel, 1986). Furthermore, in terms of accountability and transparency, XAI can decrease the application gap by discovering more information from the perspectives of various stakeholders (Frishammar et al., 2010; Arrieta et al., 2020), which allows recruiters to control or adjust the overfitted results (Jarrahi, 2018). The adjusted algorithm can convince recruiters that competitive applicants would not be eliminated by not only performing better but also informing them about the decision basis (Arrieta et al., 2020; Laurim et al., 2021). Therefore, this study suggests that explainability can contribute to augmentation in terms of anxiety.

## H2b. FAT will negatively affect anxiety.

## 3.2.3. Features Related to Anxiety

Some studies considered job relevance associated with anxiety, which is defined as “The capabilities of a system to enhance an individual's job performance” (Laurim et al., 2021, pp. 5497), when adopting an AI recruitment system. Recruiters have been using AI recruitment systems when evaluating candidates to save time by screening out applicants who do not fit in with the business. However, they have been anxious that the AI recruitment system might screen out wrong applicants. Hence, this study presumed that job relevance should be the premise for AI recruitment system adoption with the mediation of anxiety.

**H2c. Job relevance will negatively affect anxiety.**

## 3.3. Uncertainty

## 3.3.1. Replacing Uncertainty to Trust

Recruitment is an uncertain process because recruiters are requested to assess applicants based on limited information such as resumes or curriculum vitae. Although an AI recruitment system is expected to provide real-time information in uncertain situations (Jarrahi, 2018), AI without explainability may increase uncertainty. For example, recruiters may lack information when trying to track why the AI system decided to hire a specific applicant, or when the rejected applicant demands to know the reason for the decision (Ochmann & Laumer, 2019).

The non-explainable nature of AI systems in terms of uncertainty is often dealt with trust, which is defined as “the attitude that an agent will help achieve an individual’s goal in a situation characterized by uncertainty and vulnerability” (Lee & See, 2004, pp.54). For instance, Sendak et al. (2020) pointed out that human decision makers often incorporate information obtained from AI systems into their decisions without a certain understanding of the underlying information generation mechanism. Accordingly, they designed an explainable machine learning process to provide trust among stakeholders against such uncertainty. In addition, Arrieta et al. focused on the trustworthiness of XAI applications regarding the confidence in the model acting as intended to minimize the risk and uncertainty derived from the lack of information. Even if the recruiters expect a more accurate decision by adopting an AI system, the decision cannot be trusted or supported owing to uncertainties unless it is explainable.

## H3a. Trust will positively affect AI recruitment adoption.

## 3.3.2. FAT for Trust

Previous studies have stated that explainability features directly affect trust. In terms of fairness, Daft & Lengel (1986) pointed out that recruiters who recognize the fairness of the algorithm trust AI decisions more. Moreover, in terms of recruiters being accountable for not only recognizing the relevance and ethics of their decisions but also controlling the decisionmaking process to prevent unfair decisions (Newman, 1978), the controllability and openness gained through accountability could ultimately serve as the basis supporting the recruiter’s final decision, which makes the decision more confident and trustworthy (Arrieta et al., 2020). Based on these perceptions, people are more likely to trust AI systems if they can confirm the process of the algorithm (Abdul et al., 2018). That is, the transparency of an AI system can reduce the application and knowledge gaps by allowing every stakeholder to confirm and trust the basis of the decision (Ochmann & Laumer, 2019).

## H3b. FAT will positively affect trust.

## 3.3.3. Features Related to Trust

Without trust in technology, people feel insecure and desire to control technology (Parasuraman, 2000). Insecurity is defined as “the distrust of technology and skepticism about its ability to work properly” (Parasuraman, 2000, pp. 311), and has been considered along with the trustworthiness of the XAI in a similar condition to lessen the risk and uncertainty stemming from limited information (Arrieta et al., 2020). Previous studies have suggested trialability, which is defined as “the degree to which an innovation may be experimented with before adoption” (Laurim et al., 2020, pp. 5497). If recruiters lack information about the decision process of an AI system, they may want to try it, be involved in the process of building it, and compare their decisions with those made by the system, to trust it (Ochmann & Laumer, 2019). Thus, this study hypothesizes that trust can mirror insecurity and trialability as an independent variable in AI recruitment system adoption.

**H3c. Insecurity will negatively affect trust, while trialability will positively affect trust.**

## 6 4. Methodology

To verify the FAT-CAT model, we collected survey data from human resource managers from the Republic of Korea who have utilized or are considering to adopt AI recruitment systems. Participants were notified of the definitions of each construct and asked to answer them based on their experiences and knowledge. We confirmed that the participants responded voluntarily, and their identifiable personal information were not collected. The questionnaire comprised 49 items measured on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”. To assess the validity of the survey, all definitions and items were sourced from well-estimated references. The constructs and their definitions, items, and their references are described in Table 2.

## 6. Discussions

In this study, the FAT-CAT model was proposed, which explains AI system adoption by integrating explainability and augmentation features, and it was applied to AI recruitment system adoption to verify the model. It assumes that, although humans and AI must interact in terms of complexity, uncertainty, and equivocality to deal with qualitative values in decision-making, the introduction of AI without explainability can hinder these interactions. Each augmentation features were replaced with extended motivational indicators that conceptually involves it to agree with existing AI recruitment system adoption studies. Furthermore, this study investigated the path from the AI recruitment system adoption features to replaced indicators to confirm whether the latter can be representative of the former. The AI recruitment system adoption features were selected from the recruiter’s perspective because the survey targeted the recruiters. The results contain interesting findings, which are described as follows:

## 6.1. Findings Focusing on Complexity

omplexity is a feature that considers a trade-off between simplifying the task by refining unnecessary information via an AI framework and increasing the task complexity by requesting recruiters to handle the AI system. As hypothesized in H1a, complexity negatively affects AI recruitment system adoption. That is, complexity is expected to enhance the application gap by making it difficult for recruiters to foresee the adverse effect of adopting the AI recruitment system and enhance the knowledge gap by making it difficult to understand the technology. However, its explanatory power was the lowest among the significant paths to AI recruitment system adoption. We interpret that this result is owing to the presence of the AI representatives. The more complex the task is, the more efficient it is to specialize and divide the task (Hui et al., 2008); hence, a structure in which recruiters and AI representatives collaborate is often formed. In this regard, recruiters can perceive the complexity derived from interpreting the result of the AI decision, but they can pass the consideration of the complexity that arises when operating AI itself on to the AI representatives. Therefore, the negative effect of complexity may be greater if the organization requests recruiters to internalize how to operate AI, or if communication between recruiters and the AI representatives is not smooth.

The significant effect of accountability and transparency on complexity expressed in H1b may indicate that recruiters struggled when recognizing the adversities they were exposed to. In terms of controllability, recruiters may find it more difficult to discover a problematic decision basis than coming up with a solution to refine it. Explainability issues are still salient for complexity even if the task of diagnosing the problematic AI decisionmaking procedures is allocated to the AI representatives because explainability can contribute to lessening the knowledge gap between experts and non-experts through openness and transparency. Fairness, on the other hand, has an insignificant impact on complexity. Unlike accountability and transparency, in which the discovery of the decision-making procedures followed XAI could be an immediate solution, solving the fairness problem remains complex even if the explainability mitigates the complexity of discovering an unfair decision basis. Because fairness is an equivocal value, there have been various discussions in the recruitment field (e.g., discussion between subjective and objective fairness) (Köchling &

Wehner, 2020). In addition, referring to the resulting AI decision, it is somewhat easy to infer 2 whether the AI is unfair even without explainability (e.g., it was obvious that the AI 3 recruitment system of the Amazon tended to favor male applicants) (Peña et al., 2020). In 4 other words, recruiters may detect complexity when communicating enough to resolve 5 unfairness issues rather than when discovering it. Therefore, explainability did not explain 6 complexity significantly in terms of fairness. Consequently, fairness is expected to have a 7 significant effect on equivocality.

## 6.2. Findings Focusing on Anxiety

The significant effect of fairness on equivocality was considered in H2b. Anxiety refers to the idea that AI lacks the capability to manage equivocality issues included in the decision it has learned. The significant path from fairness, as well as transparency, to anxiety may imply that recruiters perceived that they could pave the way for solving equivocal issues, such as fairness, by identifying the problem through explainability. Although the process of dealing with fairness could be a complex task, recruiters may be less anxious about the wrong reference derived from the AI recruitment system, which has learned equivocal decisions.

However, contrary to our hypotheses, accountability was identified as an insignificant feature affecting anxiety. Moreover, anxiety was identified as an insignificant feature affecting the AI recruitment system adoption. During the early stages of AI recruitment adoption and when the role of AI reps and recruiters are divided, recruiters may be anxious about AI adoption regardless of its capability because they may not be fully aware of the benefits and risks (Van Esch et al., 2019). Different from fairness and transparency where recruiters can mitigate adverse effects by communicating with each other based on the information provided by the explainability, recruiters may still not think that they can directly control the AI model itself or that they can understand the ramifications of utilizing the AI model to resolve their anxiety. Therefore, explainability cannot immediately relieve the recruiter’s anxiety, but it is expected that the anxiety of recruiters will decrease in the long term if they gain experience in resolving equivocality through explainability and become accustomed to controlling the AI system through experience.

If explainability can contribute to making better decisions by improving the equivocality problems, the next-generation AI recruitment system, which will learn the decision, could create a virtuous cycle that could reduce the recruiter’s anxiety. This assumption is supported by H2c, which underlines the significant effect of job relevance on anxiety. In other words, explainability can be the beginning of a more objective and fair hiring culture in the long run.

## 6.3. Findings Focusing on Trust

Trust assumes that the more information the explainability provides, the more reliable the AI’s decision is for recruiters. In other words, without explainability, recruiters who refer to AI decisions become more uncertain and distrust the AI recruitment system. This assumption is supported by H3a and H3b. Considering that people are more likely to adopt reliable technology, trust has been identified as a key factor in technology adoption consistently in previous studies (Shin et al., 2020). The high explanatory power presented in H3a once again emphasizes the role of trust as an important feature for adopting AI recruitment systems. In addition, the significant effects of H3b suggest that explainability can contribute to the provision of information in terms of FAT. That is, explainability can provide more information about whether the algorithm is biased, whether the algorithm contains potential adverse effects, and the causality of the algorithm that involves more insights than the classification result (Ochmann & Laumer, 2019; Arrieta et al., 2020). Explainability could also mitigate the application gap by allowing recruiters to easily understand the potential adverse effects of the AI recruitment system based on the rich information it provides. Moreover, such rich information could be distributed to non-experts and stakeholders to improve the knowledge gap.

H3c supports the idea that trust is highly related to insecurity and trialability, which are the key features for adopting AI recruitment systems considered in previous studies (Laurim et al., 2021). Recruiters who lack information about an AI recruitment system may become skeptical about its adoption and may first want to try it to witness its contribution and trust it. Explainability allows recruiters to obtain direct information explicitly instead of obtaining indirect information empirically, which makes it easy for them to trust an AI recruitment system.

## 7. Contributions, Limitations, and Conclusion

In this study, the FAT-CAT model was proposed, which investigates AI system adoption with explainability and augmentation features, and it was applied to an AI recruitment system adoption case to verify its effectiveness. As a first attempt to highlight AI adoption by focusing on the possibility of cooperation between human decision makers who can consider equity and AI decision makers with high quantitative efficiency, this study suggests the following implications.

First, this study integrated the theories of explainability, human–AI augmentation, and technology adoption, which aim to achieve a common goal in terms of decision justification. Instead of focusing on the functional features of the technology that were prevalently used in existing technology adoption research, this study focused on the capability of AI systems to contribute to justifiable decisions. As a solution to the social demand for upright decisions rather than accurate decisions, the FAT-CAT model emphasizes the cooperation between human and AI decision makers and suggests explainability as a key aspect for the cooperation of these two actors. When digital transformation is delayed owing to a lack of justification, such as in the case of Amazon AI recruitment system, the FAT-CAT model can serve as a tool that suggests the right direction. Second, the FAT-CAT model could be applied to every AI system adoption case. Although the FAT-CAT model was applied to the AI recruitment system adoption representatively in this study, explainability and augmentation are important for future decisions in various fields that require equity. Regardless of the field, human decision makers may be able to justify decisions in a more sophisticated manner when they are less complex. Consequently, more information can be provided from various perspectives, and explainability may contribute to creating such conditions. Third, this study suggests major issues to be considered in digital transformation strategies. We distinguished the role of AI and human decision makers, clarified how and where they can cooperate, and highlighted the considerations when human decision makers internalize AI technologies. In the short term, where recruiters collaborate with AI representatives, recruiters were interested in the information they could obtain by the XAI rather than the complexity of using the AI. Therefore, they perceived the positive aspect of explainability in terms of problems caused by too little or too much information, but they remained anxious because they did not fully understand the AI system. On the other hand, in the long term, where they must internalize the AI system, this study anticipated that recruiters may perceive the complexity of using the AI but may be less anxious about perceiving controllability. Finally, this study suggests a virtuous cycle from the perspective of AI system adoption. It describes the structure in which a better AI system yields a better decision, and a better decision becomes the better training data fed to the AI system. In contrast to previous studies that attempted to improve the decision quality by improving the performance of the AI system (e.g., Ahsen et al., 2019), this study attempted to improve the decision quality in terms of management strategy.

However, this research should be cautiously viewed for several reasons. First, this study described the CAT model by using the extended motivational features that replace the augmentation indicators. This considers two concerns: recruiters may perceive the utility of the XAI in a motivational form instead of the conceptual form of complexity, uncertainty, and equivocality because they are unfamiliar with those concepts owing to the AI recruitment system adoption being in its early stages. Moreover, there were only few studies that focused on the direct path from augmentation features to the AI system adoption. Therefore, future studies can directly focus on the influence of complexity, uncertainty, and equivocality on technology adoption, as studies examining their relationships become more common. Second, the external features that led to the adoption of the AI system before the introduction of explainability (such as perceived usefulness or social influence) can still be key factors for the AI recruitment system adoption independently from the FAT-CAT model (e.g., Howardson & Behrend, 2014). In future studies, the relationship between the perceived importance of considering equity and significance of the FAT-CAT model should be discovered. Finally, although this study reviewed the existing literature, which stated that recruiters and applicants have different interests regarding the AI recruitment systems, this study only focused on the perspective of a recruiter. Therefore, future studies will be able to derive insights from a different point of view by focusing on the perspective of an applicant.
